query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a pack-aluminizing diffusion treatment to the cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy will form a thin, adherent alumina-rich surface layer that impedes oxygen ingress, thereby improving its oxidation resistance at high temperatures without compromising its inherent mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and acceptable high-temperature yield strength, but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Pack-aluminizing diffusion treatment to develop an Al-rich surface layer.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at high temperatures (800–1000 °C) for 5 hours under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, diffusion-induced alumina-rich surface layer formed on the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The aluminide layer reacts with ambient oxygen at elevated temperatures to form a continuous, protective alumina (Al2O3) scale that limits further oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy, thus preserving the alloy’s mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved oxidation resistance evidenced by reduced oxygen uptake and a more intact, adherent alumina scale while maintaining similar room- and high-temperature ductility and yield strength compared with untreated material.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy shows inadequate resistance against oxidation, leading to pesting or degradation under high-temperature, oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for exposures in air at 800–1000 °C for up to 5 hours and under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1; the treatment must not significantly alter the alloy’s bulk composition to preserve its mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact integrity, thickness, and long-term adherence of the alumina scale under cyclic or extended high-temperature exposure remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group will undergo a pack-aluminizing diffusion treatment and the other will remain untreated. Expose both groups to air at a selected temperature (e.g., 900 °C) for 5 hours. After exposure, perform microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM) to characterize the oxidation scale and conduct tensile tests at room and high temperatures to assess any changes in mechanical properties.
measurements: Oxygen uptake (quantitative analysis via weight gain or oxygen depth profiling)
Oxide scale thickness and adhesion (via microscopy)
Tensile ductility and yield strength before and after oxidation exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pack-aluminized samples exhibit similar oxygen uptake, oxide scale degradation, or a comparable deterioration in mechanical properties as the untreated samples, the hypothesis that the surface treatment enhances oxidation resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). After discussing the law of strength change with temperature and analyzing the results of the transmission electron microscopy, it is concluded that the deformation of the alloy at high temperature is mainly controlled by dislocation, and the morphology and density of the dislocation control the mechanical properties of the alloy. We have not discussed the plasticity change before, so the next focus is to analyze the change in alloy plasticity at high temperature and the reasons for that change. In high-temperature tensile tests, the strength of the alloy is more important, but the plasticity changes are equally important. Dual-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent room temperature and high-temperature properties have been widely studied as potential high-temperature structural materials. However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. With the increase in Hf content, the high-temperature strength and ductility of the alloy first increased and then decreased, while the room temperature performance remained almost unchanged. Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. The alloys JZ1 and JZ2 had lower Ge and Sn concentrations and the same but lower Ti concentrations than the alloys studied by Vellios and Tsakiropoulos (see []) and Li and Tsakiropoulos [] and references within and did not suffer from complete disintegration to powders, instead their scales spalled off and scale fragments disintegrated into powder. This suggests (i) that the simultaneous presence of Ge and Sn in the alloys “controlled and improved” the effect of Ge and (ii) that the synergy of these two elements with Hf, Ta, Ti, and W was also beneficial regarding control of pest oxidation. The oxidation resistance of the alloy JZ2 at 800 °C was slightly improved, most likely because of its lower vol.% of the Nbss and higher Sn+Ge content, compared with the alloy JZ1. The results of this work and the literature suggest that additional research should aim to find out whether the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys with Ta and W additions in the pest regime could be improved with simultaneous addition of Sn and Ge with Al and Cr.

The latter synergy also improved the oxidation kinetics in JZ3+ compared with the Ta and W free alloy OHS1 (parabolic + linear in OHS1, with the kp for the first 3h of oxidation [] similar to that of JZ3+ for the whole duration of the oxidation experiment). In Ti-rich (Ti ≥ 24 at.%) Sn-containing Nb-silicide-based alloys, after isothermal oxidation at 1200 °C there was enrichment in Sn in the substrate at the oxide scale/substrate interface where the compounds Nb3Sn and Nb5Sn2Si were formed [,,,]. The latter intermetallic has W5Si3 as its prototype (the same as βNb5Si3), and is not believed to be stable in the Nb-Si-Sn ternary system at 1200 °C []. The research in [,,,] would suggest that the synergy of Mo and Hf with Al and Cr, and contamination of the alloy by oxygen stabilised the Nb5Sn2Si compound at high temperatures. The Nb5Sn2Si or other TM5Sn2X compounds [] (TM = Nb, Ti, X = Al, Si) were not observed in the alloys JZ2, JZ3 and JZ3+ at 1200 °C (Table 7), which would suggest that the synergy of Sn with Ge, Ta and W did not stabilise these compounds. Multi-component refractory elements-based alloys possess a mainly BCC structure. One of the most interesting HEA types is a system with coherent BCC and B2 phases with a microstructure similar to Ni-based alloys. The difference is that the disordered BCC phase is present as cubic nanoparticles. This structure provides a combination of high strength and high plasticity at high temperatures and is standard for Al-containing multi-component alloys. Thus, for the AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr alloy, its yield strength is 745 MPa at 1000 °C, and good plasticity is preserved (the height decrease is >50% under compression) []. However, there can also be observed oxides and intermetallic phases, such as Laves phases, in the refractory HEAs that can affect the materials’ ductility. For example, in the NbCrMoTaTiZr, CrNbTiZr, and CrNbTiVZr alloys, the Laves phase is formed in the BCC-matrix because of the smaller radius of Cr in comparison to other elements [,,]. Nevertheless, in Reference [], an NbMoTaWVCr alloy with an extremely high yield strength of 3416 MPa and good plasticity of 5.3% at room temperature was obtained. decision.trend: Starting from general mechanical assessments of HfNbTaTiZr-based refractory high-entropy alloys (PMC7514121 and PMC7514597), researchers explored substituting or partially removing specific elements (e.g., Mo, V) and investigating the effects of interstitial doping on mechanical properties (PMC7299626). Most work focused on strength, ductility, and high-temperature performance (PMC10453588), but oxidation resistance remains comparatively underexplored. None has established a direct solution for preventing oxygen-driven damage in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr without changing bulk composition. Thus, the ongoing need is a method to form a robust barrier that limits O2 ingress at elevated temperatures, ensuring good strength and ductility are retained.
decision.unsolved: While minor compositional modifications or interstitial doping can enhance mechanical performance, the open challenge is to achieve significant and stable oxidation protection specifically for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr at high temperatures without altering its bulk chemistry or degrading its mechanical properties.
decision.lever: Apply a pack-aluminizing diffusion treatment on the cast alloy to deposit an Al-rich surface layer, which then forms a protective alumina scale upon exposure to high temperatures (e.g. 800–1000 °C in air). This thin diffusion-based layer should limit oxygen ingress and preserve underlying ductility while maintaining the alloy’s inherent strength.
decision.why: Prior work on related refractory HEAs has focused on mechanical and microstructural modifications, but has not directly addressed oxidation barriers in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr. A surface aluminide can create a stable oxide scale, hindering oxygen penetration and preventing pest-like attack, as suggested by broader experience with aluminide coatings on high-temperature alloys. A straightforward test would expose both treated and untreated samples to air at 800–1000 °C for 5 h under strain rates (∼10−4–10−2 s−1) and compare oxygen uptake, oxidation product morphology, and mechanical properties. Observation of similar oxygen content and surface attack in the treated sample relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
